title: Who Is Anil Chakravarthy? The Bengaluru Boy Who Became a Chancellor's Gold Medalist, an MIT PhD, a Silicon Valley CEO — and Now Adobe's Next Leader
excerpt: Adobe's board has named Anil Chakravarthy as its next president and CEO, making him the second consecutive Indian-origin leader at the helm of the creative software giant. His journey from Basavanagudi to the C-suite is a story of quiet, methodical ambition.
body:
On September 3, 2026, Adobe's board of directors announced that Anil Chakravarthy would become the company's next president and chief executive officer, effective December 1. He will succeed Shantanu Narayen, who is stepping into the role of executive chair after 18 years at the helm. For the Indian diaspora, the moment carries a particular resonance: Adobe's top job is passing from one Indian-origin leader to another, at a company whose software shapes how much of the world creates.

From Basavanagudi to Varanasi

Chakravarthy grew up in Basavanagudi, one of Bengaluru's oldest and most storied neighborhoods. After early schooling at Sudarshan Vidya Mandir and Vijaya High School, he completed his pre-university studies at National College, Basavanagudi, between 1983 and 1985.

He then moved north to Varanasi to study computer science and engineering at the Institute of Technology, Banaras Hindu University — now IIT (BHU). He graduated in 1989 with a Chancellor's Gold Medal, the university's highest academic distinction.

MIT and the Pivot to Business

At 21, Chakravarthy left India for the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He earned a master's degree and then a PhD at the MIT Media Lab, completing his doctorate in 1995. During his time at MIT, he received the MIT-Japan Science and Technology Prize for his research and also became a Certified Information Systems Security Professional.

He has described that period as a personal turning point — the moment he shifted from wanting to be a scientist to wanting to build and lead businesses. It was a pivot that would define the next three decades of his career.

""I am deeply honored to have been chosen to lead Adobe during this pivotal moment," Chakravarthy said in a statement."

Building Across Silicon Valley

Chakravarthy's first job out of MIT was at McKinsey & Company, where he spent five years and rose to become the co-leader of the E-Business Practice in the firm's Silicon Valley Business Technology Office. It was the late 1990s, the internet was rewriting every playbook, and the consulting work gave him a panoramic view of how technology companies actually operated.

From McKinsey, he moved into hands-on technology roles. A stint at startup Logictier was followed by a product management position at VeriSign, focused on enterprise security services. Then came Symantec, where he spent nearly a decade — from 2004 to 2013 — climbing through engineering, services, and product leadership. He ran divisions covering endpoint protection, encryption, mobile security, and data loss prevention, and even headed Symantec's India technical operations from Pune.

"Gaining exposure to different parts of a business would be important if I wanted to eventually lead a company."

In a 2017 podcast, Chakravarthy credited Symantec's then-CEO John Thompson with giving him the chance to step beyond engineering into services management — a move that shaped his ambition to one day run an entire company.

CEO at Informatica, Then Adobe

In 2013, Chakravarthy joined Informatica, the enterprise cloud data-management company, as executive vice president and chief product officer. He became CEO in 2015 and led the company through a major transformation to cloud and subscription services over the next five years.

His connection with Adobe developed through Informatica's partnership with the software giant, particularly around Adobe Experience Platform and data integration. When he joined Adobe in January 2020, he told CNBC that "a lot of the reason I came was the opportunity to work with Shantanu and work with the leadership team at Adobe."

At Adobe, Chakravarthy took charge of the Digital Experience business and worldwide field operations. He oversaw the development of AI-powered products including Adobe CX Enterprise, GenStudio, and Brand Visibility, and championed the acquisitions of Workfront and Semrush. Under his watch, Adobe's customer experience orchestration business became a cornerstone of the company's enterprise strategy.

Why This Moment Matters

Chakravarthy takes the CEO title at a pivotal juncture. Adobe's stock has fallen sharply since 2023, as investors worry that AI-native tools from Canva, Midjourney, and OpenAI could erode the creative software empire Narayen built. Adobe is not standing still — it has shipped AI agents for enterprise customers, Firefly models for creatives, and an agentic software vision that Chakravarthy has personally championed — but the market wants proof that the company can own AI-native creation, not just bolt it onto legacy products.

"I am deeply honored to have been chosen to lead Adobe during this pivotal moment," Chakravarthy said in a statement. "I'm energized by the opportunity to fuel growth and drive Adobe's leadership in the next era of agentic software for creativity, productivity, and customer experience."

His appointment was not without drama. The other finalist was David Wadhwani, Adobe's president of creativity and productivity and a 19-year company veteran. After the board chose Chakravarthy, Wadhwani announced his departure to pursue entrepreneurship.

Diaspora Significance

With Chakravarthy's appointment, Adobe becomes the rare American tech giant to have consecutive Indian-origin CEOs. Narayen, who joined Adobe in 1998 and became CEO in 2007, transformed the company from a boxed-software maker into a subscription and enterprise powerhouse. The baton now passes to another IIT-to-MIT pipeline product who built his career across cybersecurity, data management, and enterprise AI.

The broader pattern is unmistakable. Indian-origin executives now lead Microsoft, Alphabet, IBM, Palo Alto Networks, and soon Adobe. For families in Basavanagudi and Varanasi and every Indian neighborhood in between, Chakravarthy's story is another data point in a thesis that grows harder to ignore: that the path from an Indian classroom to a global boardroom has never been shorter.
